title: The Integration of Law into Global Business Solutions: The Rise, Transformation, and Potential Future of the Big Four Accountancy Networks in the Global Legal Services Market
pub: Law & Social Inquiry, Vol. 43, Issue 3, Summer 2018, pp. 981–1026
author: David B. Wilkins · Maria J. Esteban Ferrer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The source does not assess whether stronger in-house power and business integration improve accountability while increasing professional-capture risks, nor does it advance reciprocal duties or contextual regulation. It instead redirects attention to how commercially oriented corporate demand, outsourcing and process integration may advantage the Big Four, while treating broader displacement as a prediction rather than an established outcome.
qs: Thus, corporate clients are increasingly demanding that their legal advisors understand their business, work collaboratively with business leaders and other professionals, and generally justify their service in terms of its contribution to the bottom line.

Whether all these trends result in the “End of Lawyers” (Susskind 2008) or the “Death of Big Law” (Ribstein 2010), as some scholars have predicted with growing apocalyptic fervor, they are very likely to further the legal ambitions of the Big Four.

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s integration-over-replacement framing and materially develops it by tracing the Big Four’s shift from separate legal networks to multidisciplinary business-solutions models. It also supplies historical and regulatory evidence while explicitly leaving actual delivery quality, dominance and law-firm displacement unresolved.
qs: Although it is far from certain the extent to which the Big Four will be able to displace law firms and other established providers in many areas, their growing size, sophistication, and increased transparency on the Internet seems likely to further the integration of law—and therefore legal providers—into global business processes that lie outside the control of lawyers.

st.t: Global legal markets: Liberalization remains locally contested
st.an: The source accepts that globalization and regulatory change expand legal-services markets, and materially develops the cluster by identifying specific mechanisms—deregulation, regulatory gaps, transnational trade pressure, and provider lobbying—that enable Big Four expansion. Its prediction of further liberalization is qualified rather than inevitable, remaining compatible with the cluster’s account of locally contested opening.
qs: together, the trend toward deregulation in many advanced economies and the regulatory gaps in many emerging ones have made it easier for the Big Four to expand their legal services offerings.

st.t: Provider convergence: Buyers coordinate an unbundled market
st.an: The source accepts the convergence thesis by portraying the Big Four as combining legal, business, technology and project-management capabilities and by describing post-SOX unbundling. It materially extends the cluster by identifying recruitment and talent development as capabilities supporting this integrated-delivery model, while treating efficiency gains as objectives rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Finally, in addition to promising greater integration of law and business, and new and more attractive approaches to talent development, the Big Four are also attempting to leverage their expertise in technology and project management to develop innovative approaches to delivering legal services that build on the disruptive innovations of tomorrow.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not evaluate generative AI’s jagged capabilities, verification needs or task-level performance, but it materially extends the cluster’s operating-model thesis. Its longitudinal account shows legal delivery already shifting toward multidisciplinary, process-integrated business models combining legal expertise, technology and other professional capabilities, while cautioning that claimed integration may exceed operational reality.
qs: By combining their core professional services (assurance, advisory, and tax and legal) with new capabilities such as strategy consulting, on-demand talent models, cognitive technologies, cloud computing, digital applications, cyber security, and crisis services, the Big Four appear to be following a similar strategy.

But even if the accountancy network’s new integrated solutions model is currently more rhetoric than reality, the Big Four are nevertheless using this rhetoric to attempt to gain a competitive advantage over law firms.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of workflow unbundling, outsourcing, process management and buyer pressure for efficient, commercially oriented delivery. It materially extends that proposition by identifying the Big Four’s integrated multidisciplinary structure, technology capabilities and regulatory openings as a specific provider-side model positioned to benefit, while treating displacement of law firms as uncertain.
qs: Although it is far from certain the extent to which the Big Four will be able to displace law firms and other established providers in many areas, their growing size, sophistication, and increased transparency on the Internet seems likely to further the integration of law—and therefore legal providers—into global business processes that lie outside the control of lawyers.

kp.k: Historical evidence establishes context, not AI displacement findings
kp.d: The article examines the Big Four’s post-Sarbanes-Oxley expansion and organizational transformation, principally through website research in 2011–2012 and 2015, supplemented by archival material and subsequent examples. Its central argument concerns integrated legal and business services; AI appears as one emerging capability rather than as a measured cause of lawyer displacement.
qs: this article documents the rise and transformation of the Big Four legal service lines since the enactment of the Sarbanes Oxley Act of 2002.
Finally, the global Web sites of PwC, Deloitte, KPMG, and EY were revisited in November 2015, following the same process as in March 2012.

kp.k: Website evidence measures presentations, not verified service delivery
kp.d: Researchers examined 151 PwC, 123 Deloitte, 102 KPMG and 115 EY location sites, alongside affiliated or associated law-firm websites and press archives. Initial collection ran from July 2011 to February 2012, with a March 2012 update. The authors explicitly limit their descriptive findings: advertised practices and ambitions do not establish actual delivery or quality.
qs: the analysis is largely descriptive and relies heavily on the use of frequencies and percentages.

We therefore make no representation, for example, about whether the legal services that the Big Four claim to offer in any particular legal market are, in fact, being delivered, or whether their legal work is of high quality.
At a minimum, the Web presence we document reveals the Big Four’s ambitions for their legal services arms—as well as what they think will appeal to potential clients.

kp.k: Legal networks expanded beyond tax and Europe
kp.d: In March 2012, PwC promoted legal services in 124 countries, Deloitte in ninety-seven, KPMG in seventy-three and EY in twenty-nine. The authors distinguish full legal practices (FLPs), advertising a broad range of services, from nascent legal practices (NLPs), showing more limited references beyond tax; NLP identification criteria differ by network. FLP country counts rose from 70 to 85 for PwC, 49 to 69 for Deloitte, 39 to 53 for KPMG and 23 to 69 for EY between March 2012 and November 2015. These are advertised geographic footprints, not measured market shares.
qs: PwC was promoting legal services in 124 countries worldwide, Deloitte in ninety-seven countries, KPMG in seventy-three countries, and EY in twenty-nine countries.
Most notably, since March 2012, EY has increased 200 percent the number of countries where its member firms offer FLP
Because the Big Four have differing approaches to the marketing of their NLPs on the Web, the criteria by which certain countries have been included as having NLPs also differ by network

kp.k: Integrated solutions replaced imitation of traditional law firms
kp.d: The authors distinguish five stages: nascent MDPs in the 1980s; federal MDPs in the 1990s–2000; crisis and renewal in 2001–2004; integrated MDPs in 2005–2011; and integrated solutions from 2012 onward. Whereas earlier legal networks sought independent law-firm identities, later models embedded lawyers in common brands, processes, risk controls and multidisciplinary client teams. The authors qualify the extent of achieved integration, noting scholarship that questions whether organizational rhetoric matches reality.
qs: In the 1990s, the accounting firms attempted to enter the legal services market by aping the ways of large law firms

the Big Four are moving aggressively to integrate their FLPs within their international networks, thereby subjecting them to the same hierarchical controls, branding, strategy, processes, standards, and values as the rest of the business.

But even if the accountancy network’s new integrated solutions model is currently more rhetoric than reality, the Big Four are nevertheless using this rhetoric to attempt to gain a competitive advantage over law firms.

kp.k: Auditor restrictions left substantial opportunities for legal expansion
kp.d: The authors argue that SOX restricted specified nonaudit services to US-listed audit clients rather than prohibiting diversified accounting firms. Ambiguous service boundaries, uneven enforcement and continued tax work permitted overlapping advisory activity. More importantly, companies that were not audit clients remained potential legal clients, subject to applicable legal-profession regulation. European variation and incomplete restrictions also supported expansion.
qs: Contrary to popular perception, Section 201 of SOX did not establish an audit-firm-only rule.

the real growth in the development of each of the Big Four’s legal networks has come from their ability to sell legal services to the vast majority of companies around the world that are not their audit clients.
Nothing in SOX prohibits this practice.

kp.k: Legal deregulation enabled multidisciplinary ownership and service integration
kp.d: The article identifies ABS authorization, reductions in activities reserved to lawyers and shifts from professional associations to independent regulators as facilitating Big Four entry. It describes the Legal Services Act 2007 and SRA licensing as enabling integrated practices in England and Wales, while regulatory ambiguity offered opportunities in jurisdictions such as China. These are jurisdiction-specific mechanisms, not evidence that nonlawyer ownership or legal practice was universally permitted.
qs: the creation of alternative business structures (ABSs) that allow lawyers and nonlawyers to go into business together in fully integrated multidisciplinary practices, and nonlawyers to invest in and manage law firms
the reduction of activities that are exclusively reserved for licensed lawyers
a shift in the control of the professions from professional associations to independent regulators
Taking advantage of this regulatory ambiguity, Deloitte China markets the provision of legal services through Qin Li Law Firm

kp.k: Global scale and fragmentation favored new provider competition
kp.d: Citing published estimates, the authors report 72 percent global legal-market growth between 2005 and 2014, including 6 percent since the 2008 crisis, to around $618 billion. They contrast this fragmented market with audit concentration and argue that multinational demand for consistent cross-border services favors the Big Four’s reach and integration. A hypothetical capture of 1 percent of the forecast $726.2 billion market for 2019 illustrates potential scale, not an observed outcome.
qs: between 2005 and 2014 the global legal services market grew by 72 percent—including a 6 percent increase since the financial crisis of 2008—reaching a total value of around $618 billion
the turnover jointly generated by all the top law firms ranked in the Am Law 100 for the same year (American Lawyer 2015) accounted for a scant 13 percent of the global legal market.
they have increasingly looked for professional service firms that can provide them with consistent services—including legal services—across their entire platform

kp.k: Premium law-firm specialization opened operational legal service opportunities
kp.d: The authors argue that elite firms’ pursuit of high-margin deals and litigation encouraged withdrawal from employment, property and general corporate work, creating openings for multidisciplinary providers. The Big Four’s alternative emphasizes helping clients operate businesses rather than exclusively winning exceptional matters. The 2017 PwC–GE tax agreement illustrates this model: PwC would hire more than 600 GE tax personnel and acquire tax technologies to provide global enterprise managed tax services.
qs: The mantra was “premium work for premium clients,” exiting commodity businesses to concentrate on high-margin work

Instead of focusing all their attention on landing the “bet the company” case, the Big Four are leveraging the full range of their knowledge and expertise to develop innovative business solutions to help their clients “run the company” efficiently and effectively.
PwC will hire more than 600 of GE’s highly regarded tax team members from around the world and acquire GE’s tax technologies

kp.k: Technology and outsourcing supported integrated delivery strategies
kp.d: The article links routine-service efficiency to IT-enabled project management, offshoring and unbundling. It cites Deloitte’s 2014 acquisition of managed document-review provider ATD Legal, its 2016 Conduit Law transaction involving outsourced lawyers, and its 2016 Kira Systems alliance. The article’s narrative describes Conduit as an acquisition, whereas its cited press-release title describes an affiliation. Kira CEO Noah Waisberg’s assertion about deployment scale is a company claim, not an independent measure of AI effectiveness or labor substitution.
qs: sophisticated IT-enabled project management systems
In 2014, Deloitte acquired ATD Legal, one of the few providers of managed document review services in Canada
Deloitte Announces Affiliation with Conduit Law.
That same year, Deloitte announced that it was forming an alliance with Kira Systems
the largest professional services AI [artificial intelligence] deployment anywhere, period

kp.k: Technology alliances signal ambitions beyond conventional professional boundaries
kp.d: Examples include PwC–Google in 2014, KPMG–McLaren in 2014, EY–LinkedIn in 2015 and Deloitte–Apple in 2016. The authors interpret these as efforts to combine professional expertise with analytics, cognitive technologies, cloud computing and digital applications. They expressly leave their effects on legal businesses unresolved rather than treating alliance announcements as demonstrated transformation.
qs: We bring in the content, they bring in the technology
It remains to be seen how these moves will impact the Big Four’s global legal businesses.

By combining their core professional services (assurance, advisory, and tax and legal) with new capabilities such as strategy consulting, on-demand talent models, cognitive technologies, cloud computing, digital applications, cyber security, and crisis services, the Big Four appear to be following a similar strategy.

kp.k: Talent competition extends beyond hiring established law-firm partners
kp.d: The authors describe lateral recruitment from major firms alongside leadership predominantly developed within the Big Four. They argue that multidisciplinary teamwork, employment conditions and career opportunities can attract lawyers dissatisfied with traditional firms. Evidence includes Deloitte Legal’s Czech student-employer recognition, Taj’s gender-equality award and the authors’ observations of graduate recruitment; these do not establish universal comparative employment advantages or AI-related headcount effects.
qs: the leaders of the Big Four’s legal teams are primarily individuals who have spent the majority of their careers inside one of these institutions.
for two years in a row Deloitte Legal was recognized as the most attractive law firm employer by Czech law students
the Big Four are increasingly able to recruit top students directly out of law school in many jurisdictions

kp.k: Reduced lawyer oversight remains a reported technological prediction
kp.d: The conclusion reports Susskind’s and Ribstein’s argument that cost pressures and more sophisticated IT could embed legal advice in business processes, allowing legally trained business personnel to operate with limited lawyer oversight. The authors do not establish that this occurred or endorse the inevitable end of lawyers; they argue instead that such trends would likely benefit integrated providers while acknowledging law-firm adaptation and uncertain competitive outcomes.
qs: may very well lead many commercial clients to seek to integrate legal advice directly into business processes through “smart” systems capable of being used by “legally trained” business people with minimal oversight and supervision by formally trained lawyers.
Law firms, however, are unlikely to go gently into the good night some have predicted for them.

Further research will be needed to determine how PwC, KPMG, Deloitte, and EY navigate the professional, managerial, and technological challenges inherent in deploying their new integrated solution business model

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors present AI and related technologies as components of the Big Four’s emerging integrated business-solutions model, rather than as a demonstrated replacement for lawyers.
pts.d: Wilkins and Esteban Ferrer argue that the Big Four are combining legal expertise, technology and project management to develop more efficient legal services and broader business solutions. They cite Deloitte’s 2016 Kira Systems alliance as evidence of this strategic direction. The description of that alliance as the largest professional-services AI deployment is explicitly attributed in the article to Kira CEO Noah Waisberg, not established as an independent finding. In their conclusion, the authors discuss a conditional prospect, drawing on Susskind and Ribstein: cost pressures and increasingly sophisticated information technology could embed legal advice in business processes used by legally trained business people with little lawyer supervision. Their own more definite prediction is that these broader developments are likely to advance the Big Four’s legal-market ambitions. These are claims about AI alongside other technologies and organizational changes, not findings isolating AI’s effects. Relevant passages appear on pp. 1006–1009 in the supplied text.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of corporate announcements, organizational examples and cited scholarship, not measured AI performance or demonstrated AI-driven market effects.
pts.d: The specific AI example is Deloitte’s announced Kira alliance in 2016. Other examples include managed document review, outsourced-lawyer services and alliances with technology companies. These illustrate investments and ambitions rather than quantified improvements attributable to AI. The article’s larger empirical foundation is descriptive research into Big Four and affiliated-law-firm websites collected in 2011–2012 and revisited in 2015, supplemented by archival press material. The authors expressly limit what such self-presentations establish: they do not verify delivery or quality of advertised legal services. The smart-systems scenario rests on cited arguments by Susskind and Ribstein rather than an original technology study. No AI accuracy benchmark, productivity experiment or displacement estimate is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes technological investments already underway by 2016 but leaves their legal-market consequences open and makes future transformation conditional on costs, technological development and implementation.
pts.d: The authors locate the emerging integrated-solutions model in the period since 2012 and discuss technology alliances announced during 2014–2016. They give no deadline for AI-enabled transformation. The possible shift toward business-operated smart legal systems depends on continuing cost pressure and predicted gains in information technology. They explicitly state that the effect of the alliances on the Big Four’s legal businesses remains unknown and call for further research into the professional, managerial and technological challenges of implementation. The article does not endorse the disappearance of lawyers or large law firms as an established outcome.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate clients, Big Four legal-service providers, traditional law firms and the lawyers or business professionals involved in corporate legal work.
pts.d: Corporate clients are envisaged as receiving legal support embedded in ongoing business operations, including routine work, rather than only standalone advice on exceptional transactions or litigation. The Big Four could strengthen their competitive position through combined legal, technological and operational capabilities. Traditional law firms face competition from that broader service model. Under the conditional smart-systems scenario discussed by the authors, legally trained business personnel could perform activities with reduced supervision by formally trained lawyers. The article connects Deloitte’s investments particularly to North American and UK markets, within a wider global corporate-services strategy. It does not offer specific AI predictions about access to justice, junior-lawyer employment or legal staffing ratios.
